---
title: Postprocessing
description: "Turn the nested prediction table into the columns an application consumes."
---

A postprocessor turns the [prediction table](../reference/prediction-output.qmd) into the
shape an application needs. It receives and returns an eager Polars DataFrame.

Suppose an application needs one list of dispute probabilities and one list
of review decisions for each account-review observation. Reuse `model` from
[Train and save](../learn/train-and-save.qmd), with a `/trxns/disputed`
target on every retained transaction. This processor converts its
[nested prediction output](../reference/prediction-output.qmd) into those
application columns:

```python
import polars as pl
import relflow as rf

@rf.postprocess
def decision(frame: pl.DataFrame, *, threshold: float) -> pl.DataFrame:
    transactions = pl.col("predictions").struct.field("trxns")
    probability = (
        pl.element()
        .struct.field("disputed")
        .struct.field("content")
        .struct.field("probability")
    )
    return frame.select(
        payment_id=pl.col("inputs").struct.field("payment_id"),
        dispute_probabilities=transactions.list.eval(probability),
        review=transactions.list.eval(probability >= threshold),
    )

# The request file is supplied by the application.
requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    predict="payments/history/requests.parquet",
    retain=("payment_id",),
)
model.predict(
    datamodule=requests,
    batch_size=256,
    devices=1,
    callbacks=[rf.Writer(
        "payment-decisions",
        postprocessor=decision.partial(threshold=0.8),
    )],
    return_predictions=False,
)
```

The chain of `struct.field` calls follows the nesting of one output record:
`predictions`, then `trxns`, then each transaction's `disputed`, `content`,
and `probability`. `list.eval` applies that path to every transaction in the
list, so the observation keeps one row with one value per transaction. The Writer
applies the processor to each prediction batch and writes Parquet files under
`payment-decisions`. Each output list follows the retained transaction order. One output record has this shape; values are placeholders:

```yaml
payment_id: payment-42
dispute_probabilities:
  - <probability of true>
  - <probability of true>
  - <probability of true>
review:
  - <true or false>
  - <true or false>
  - <true or false>
```

The direct in-memory prediction API accepts `postprocess=` on the prediction
call. It applies the processor to the combined result once, after all model
batches have completed. A Writer applies it to each output batch.

The threshold is an application decision rule. The example uses the content
probability; incorporate the predicted value state when your application needs
to treat missingness separately. Select the threshold on validation data for
the team's review capacity and error costs; `0.8` here illustrates configuration.

## Compose and reuse

The first callback parameter must be `frame`; additional parameters are
keyword-only and bound with `.partial(...)`. A tuple of decorated processors
runs left to right. The pipeline converts Arrow to Polars before its first
stage and back to Arrow after its last.

Use the same configured processor in each output path:

```python
processor = decision.partial(threshold=0.8)
writer = rf.Writer("payment-predictions", postprocessor=processor)
deployment = rf.Deployment(model=model, retain=("payment_id",)).postprocess(processor)
```

For `Writer`, configure `retain=("payment_id",)` on the prediction data module.
Serving requires `relflow[serving]`.

Processors may change rows or columns, but must return an eager frame with at
least one column. Retain every source column they need; source data is not
otherwise available in the written table. A `Writer` requires the same output
schema across batches in its shard.

HTTP serving has an additional requirement: preserve one final row per valid
request with the same identity and order. RelFlow checks the count; processors
own identity and order, including when row counts happen to be equal.

For file output at scale, see [Batch inference](batch-inference.qmd); for the
HTTP path, see [Serving](serving.qmd).
